exp.5:8:
It says that those who insist on getting rich end up trapped. Those desires drag the person toward ruin, "perdición y muerte," that is, a deep destruction. The verse speaks of those who "want" to get rich, that is, of the ambition that rules the heart, not of having money in itself.

The apostle Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader of the church in Ephesus. Earlier he reminded him that we bring nothing into the world and take nothing out, and that we should be content with having food and clothing. Then he warns that the love of money leads people away from the faith.

Today we can ask ourselves whether the desire to have more takes away our peace, our time with God, or our generosity. A good practice is to be thankful for what we already have and to give joyfully to someone who needs it.
exp.1:13:
It says that Adam was not deceived by the serpent, but that the woman, when she was seduced, fell into disobedience. The phrase "envuelta en transgresión" means that she was caught up in sin, so the wording about being "in the transgression" means that she was caught up in sin. Christians understand in different ways what Paul means by this, since the text is brief.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young coworker who led the church in Ephesus. He gives instructions about order and teaching in the community, and he draws on the account in Genesis 3. Scholars disagree about whether he is speaking of a local situation, with false teachers in Ephesus, or of a rule for all churches. It should be read with humility.

For today: all of us can be deceived, men and women alike. For that reason it is good to examine what we hear in the light of the Bible, to live with humility, and to remain in faith, love, and holiness.
exp.2:3:
It says that the overseer, that is, the leader or pastor of the church, must manage his own household well. His children must live in submission, which means obedience and respect, and with all dignity, that is, with seriousness, honor and good behavior.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He gives requirements for those who would lead the congregation. The next verse explains the reason: the way a person cares for a family shows how he might care for the church. Some think the phrase applies to children still under his care, although the text gives no further detail.

For today: whoever serves others must begin at home. Give time to your family, teach with patience and by your example, and treat your loved ones with respect and love, without harshness.
exp.5:19:
Paul says that Timothy must guard with firmness what God entrusted to him: the message of the gospel and the work of serving the church. He must turn away from empty chatter, conversations that are worthless and have no spiritual value, and from arguments about what is falsely called knowledge, that is, ideas that claimed to be knowledge but were not. Turning away here means keeping one's distance.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was in charge of the church in Ephesus. As he finishes his letter, he gives him a final warning. Some, according to the next verse, had strayed from the faith by following these ideas. Scholars debate which specific teaching is meant, and it is not known for certain.

Today we can ask ourselves which voices influence us. Before accepting an idea, let us compare it with what the Bible teaches. And let us devote more time to the Word than to discussions that do not build up.
exp.4:24:
He says that people's good works, sooner or later, become clearly visible. Some are evident right away ("already manifest" means they can be seen at a glance). And those that are not good cannot remain hidden forever either.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, giving him advice to guide the church. In the verses before this, he speaks of choosing and evaluating leaders with care. Some sins become apparent quickly; others come to light later. With this verse he completes the thought: both the good and the bad in someone's character end up being seen. Some understand that it refers to those who would be appointed as leaders.

Today it encourages us not to lose heart if no one notices our simple service, because God sees it and in time it will be seen. It also warns us that what is hidden cannot be sustained. Let us live with sincerity, without pretending.
exp.4:6:
It says that Timothy must "give in charge" these things, that is, announce them, command them, and teach them clearly. The purpose is that they may be "blameless": that no one would have grounds to accuse or reproach the people Paul spoke about. "Blameless" here refers to a fault that others could point out.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who looks after the church in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke about widows who have no one to support them and how they should live. Some think "these things" are the instructions about widows; others think they also include what was said about families. What follows, about caring for one's own, supports both readings.

Today, the church's teachings must be stated clearly and lived out with integrity. If something is important, let us not leave it half-done: let us explain it with love and practice it, so that our lives give no reason for reproach.
exp.3:3:
He says that everything God made is good, and that nothing should be rejected if it is received with thanks to God. The first word here means "made," and the second means "to reject or throw away." The phrase about thanks means giving thanks, expressing gratitude.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who cares for the church in Ephesus. Earlier, he warned that some would falsely teach people to forbid marriage and certain foods. Paul answers that these prohibitions do not come from God. The verses that follow say that what is created is set apart for God through his word and prayer.

For today: enjoy with gratitude what God gives you, such as food, marriage, or rest, without feeling guilty about human rules that God has not placed. Before eating, or when receiving something good, give thanks to God. Still, use everything with wisdom and without excess.
exp.4:22:
Paul tells Timothy to stop drinking only water and to use a little wine, because he has stomach problems and gets sick often. "From now on" means "from now on," and "use" means "take," in small amounts.

Paul, the apostle, is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Just before this, he had asked Timothy for purity and care in his decisions. This advice is personal and practical, almost like a parenthesis. The water of that time was probably not always safe, though the Bible does not explain this, so that is only a possibility.

God cares about our bodies. Looking after our health, resting, and seeking medical help is not a lack of faith. This advice was given to Timothy, so today it is wise to ask a doctor for guidance and to live with wisdom and moderation.
exp.2:10:
It says that the women too must have good character. "Grave" means worthy of respect, serious, and of clean conduct. The ones who speak badly of others should not be gossips or slanderers. "Sober" means balanced, with self-control. "Faithful in all things" speaks of people who can be trusted with everything entrusted to them.

Paul writes to Timothy to teach him how to organize the church in Ephesus. He speaks of the deacons and their requirements. The word "women" can refer to the wives of the deacons or to women who served as deaconesses. Scholars understand it in both ways, and the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: watch your words. Before you comment on something about another person, ask yourself whether it is true, whether it helps, and whether you would say it in front of them.
exp.4:0:
It says that Paul asks Timothy not to rebuke an older man harshly, but to appeal to him with respect, as if he were his own father. Younger men he should treat as brothers. "Rebuke" means to correct with force; "exhort" means to encourage and advise.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was leading the church in Ephesus. Timothy had to correct mistakes, and Paul teaches him to do so in a familial way. The passage goes on to speak of older and younger women, always with purity. Scholars understand "elder" here to refer to an older man, though some think it could also include the leaders of the church.

For today: when you have to correct someone, do it with respect and affection, as you would with your own family. Seek to build up, not to humiliate.
exp.1:7:
Paul says that he desires the men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands, that is, with a clean life before God. And that they do so without anger or quarrels. The word "doubting" in the verse means disputing or quarreling.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just spoken of Christ giving himself for all, so he asks for prayer for all people. Now he teaches how believers should pray. Lifting up the hands was a common posture of prayer at that time. What matters is not the gesture but a clean heart at peace with others.

Before praying, examine your heart. If you hold a grudge or have an unresolved quarrel, ask God for forgiveness and seek peace with that person. In this way your prayer comes out sincere and unhindered.
exp.0:5:
Explains that some, by losing sight of the true purpose of Christian teaching (love, a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith), have turned aside to empty talk, conversation without profit. The word translated here as "turned aside unto vain jangling" means to go off course or wander away from the goal.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was in Ephesus caring for the church. Some there were arguing about myths and endless lists of ancestors, and wanted to present themselves as teachers of the law without understanding it well. Paul wants Timothy to correct this, because those discussions were not building anyone up.

For today: before entering a debate about faith, ask yourself whether it leads you to love God and people more. If it only feeds pride or argument, it is better to return to what is essential.
exp.4:15:
It says that if a believer, man or woman, has widows in their family, they should care for them personally. This way the church does not carry that burden and can help the widows who are truly alone and have no one else.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who led the church in Ephesus. Earlier he explained that the church should support widows who are truly without support, and that family members have the responsibility first (vv. 3-8). This verse repeats that idea: the family takes care of its own, and the church's resources are kept for those who have no one to look after them.

For today: if someone in your family is elderly or in need, look for ways to help them with your time, visits, or money before expecting others to do it. In this way the community can support those who have no one.
exp.0:1:
Paul greets Timothy and calls him "my true son in the faith," meaning someone who truly shares Paul's same faith in Jesus. He wishes him three blessings: grace (God's undeserved favor), mercy (his compassion), and peace. All of this comes from God the Father and from Christ Jesus, whom he calls "our Lord."

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, a young co-worker whom he left in Ephesus to look after the church. The verses that follow show that there were teachers teaching different doctrines. The phrase "son in the faith" suggests a close relationship; many think Paul had a great influence on his Christian life, although the Bible does not give all the details.

Today we can encourage others in the faith with sincere affection. Before correcting or teaching, it is worth reminding them that God gives them grace, mercy, and peace. Think of someone you can bless this week with a word of encouragement.
exp.3:10:
Paul tells Timothy: "These things command and teach." The word "command" means to order with authority, and "teach" means to instruct clearly. He is referring to what he has just said: that God is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe, and that because of this hope it is worth working and suffering.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, a young leader who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Paul wants to encourage him to teach the truths of the gospel firmly, in the face of false teachings. In the next verse he asks him that no one despise his youth, but that he be an example by his life. There are different ways to understand "especially of those who believe," but all of them emphasize that salvation is received through faith.

Teach what the Bible says with firmness, but also with humility and a good example. What you say will carry more weight if your way of living supports it.
exp.1:12:
It says that God formed Adam first and then Eve, just as Genesis 2 tells it. The phrase "was formed" simply means that God created him. Paul uses this order of creation as the reason for what he has just said in the previous verse.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his co-worker, who was looking after the church in Ephesus. There were false teachings and disorder there. Paul gives instructions for the life of the church. Christians understand this passage in different ways: some think it sets a permanent order for leadership, and others think it responds to particular problems in Ephesus. For that reason it is wise to read it with humility.

For today: whatever your position, practice service with humility and respect, study all of Scripture before drawing conclusions, and listen patiently to those who think differently.
exp.3:14:
This verse asks Timothy to think carefully about what Paul has taught him and to devote himself fully to it. "Meditate" means to reflect deeply, and "give thyself" means to commit yourself steadily. "Profiting" is an old-fashioned word meaning progress or growth. The goal is that everyone can see how Timothy is growing.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who cares for the church in Ephesus. He reminds him to use well his gift, that is, the ability God gave him to serve, and to devote himself to reading the Scriptures, encouraging others, and teaching. His growth would be a good example for the congregation.

For today: set aside a fixed time each day to read a Bible passage, think about it, and put it into practice. In this way, your growth will show in how you treat others.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that Paul and his companions work hard and endure insults and mistreatment, because their hope is set on the living God. He is the Savior of all people, meaning that salvation is offered to every person, and in a special way he saves those who believe in him.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he said that living in godliness, that is, honoring God in everyday life, is worth more than physical exercise alone. Here he explains why the effort is worthwhile: God is faithful. Some debate how to understand "Savior of all"; the most common view is that it describes an open offer to everyone, which only those who believe receive.

Today, when living out your faith costs you effort or mockery, remember that your hope is not in the approval of people, but in the living God. That gives you strength to keep going.
exp.0:16:
This verse is a song of praise to God. Paul calls him "King eternal," that is, the King who reigns through all ages. He says that God is "immortal" (he does not die), "invisible" (he cannot be seen with the eyes), and "the only wise God" (the only one with perfect wisdom). He asks that honour and glory be given to him forever.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker. He has just told how God showed mercy to him, even though he considers himself the worst of sinners. As he thinks about that grace, Paul cannot hold back and breaks out in worship. Then he goes back to giving instructions to Timothy.

For today: when you remember how God has forgiven and helped you, do not stop at the memory. Give him thanks out loud, in your own words, and let your gratitude become worship.
exp.4:8:
It says that a widow should be placed on a list or "special class" of the church only if she is at least sixty years old and has been the wife of one husband. The phrase "placed in the special class" means that she was entered into a register. The expression "wife of one husband" is understood in several ways: faithfulness in marriage, or simply a life of good testimony.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was overseeing the church in Ephesus. Earlier he speaks of helping widows who are truly in need and of families caring for their own. It is not entirely clear whether that list was for receiving help, for a service in the church, or for both. Scholars discuss this.

For today: the church and the family must care responsibly and justly for the most vulnerable. Think of a widow or an older adult you know and offer them concrete help, such as a visit, a meal, or accompanying them to an appointment.
exp.5:3:
He says that the person who teaches something different from the sound words of Jesus is puffed up with pride and in truth understands nothing. He becomes obsessed with arguments and quarrels over words. From this come envy, disputes, insults, and evil suspicions about others.

The apostle Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who led the church in Ephesus. Paul wants to protect him from teachers who were replacing the teaching of Christ with fruitless debates. According to the context, some of them were using religion to make money.

For today: before entering a discussion about faith, ask yourself whether you want to help someone or only to win and look impressive. If you notice pride, envy, or suspicion growing in you, leave the debate, return to the words of Jesus, and respond with humility and love.
exp.2:12:
For they who serve well, that is, those who faithfully carry out their ministry (the word refers to the service of the deacons), gain two things: a good standing, which is a worthy position or a good name, and great confidence, that is, assurance and courage, in the faith that centers on Christ Jesus.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just given the requirements for deacons and their families. This verse shows the value of that service. Some understand "good standing" as respect in the community; others, as a place of greater responsibility or a reward from God. The text does not fully make this clear.

Serving with humility and faithfulness, even in small things, strengthens our own faith. When we serve others, we learn to trust Christ more.
exp.4:20:
Paul speaks to Timothy with great seriousness. "I charge you" means "I solemnly order you," and he says it as if God, the Lord Jesus Christ, and the chosen angels were present. He asks him to carry out these instructions without prejudging anyone, and not to act with partiality, that is, without favoring one side over another.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just given him instructions for handling accusations against the elders and for correcting those who sin. That is why he insists that he do it with fairness. The "chosen angels" most likely refers to the angels faithful to God, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: when you have to correct, decide, or judge something, whether in the family, at work, or in the church, listen to the facts and treat everyone with the same fairness, regardless of whether you like them or not.
exp.3:12:
He says that Timothy should devote himself earnestly to three tasks while Paul is on his way: reading, exhorting, and teaching. "Give attention to" means to devote oneself with care and steadiness. "Reading" refers above all to the public reading of the Scriptures in the gathering of believers. "Exhorting" is encouraging and advising. "Teaching" is explaining the truth clearly.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader who cares for the church in Ephesus. He gives him practical instructions so that he will lead with firmness, even though some may see him as young. Paul hopes to visit him soon, but he does not want the spiritual work to stop in the meantime.

For today: if you serve in your church or your family, do not depend on improvising. Set aside time each week to read the Bible, to encourage someone with it, and to share what you have learned with others.
exp.5:17:
It says that people with money should do good, be rich in good works, be generous, and be ready to share. The explanation of the word "generous" that appears here is dropped, since the reader's verse does not use that word. The phrase about sharing without much difficulty simply means they should share what they have without much hesitation.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Just before this, he warns the rich not to be proud or to trust in money, which is uncertain, but in God, who gives everything. This verse shows how to live out that trust: using what you have to bless others.

For today: no matter how much you have, whether a lot or a little, ask yourself this week to whom you can help with your money, your time, or your things. Give with joy and simplicity, remembering that everything comes from God.
exp.2:1:
This verse lists the qualities a bishop should have, that is, the person entrusted with caring for and leading a local church. "Blameless" means that no one can rightly accuse him of a serious fault. "The husband of one wife" is understood in several ways: faithfulness in marriage, or not having more than one wife; scholars do not fully agree. "Vigilant" means alert and attentive; "sober," self-controlled; "of good behaviour," orderly and respectable; "given to hospitality," one who opens his home; "apt to teach," able to explain the Word.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was serving in Ephesus. He wants the church to have leaders of proven character, so that the gospel will be well taught and well represented before everyone.

For today: before seeking a place of service, take care of your character. Strive to be someone trustworthy at home, kind to others, and willing to learn the Bible so that you can share it with humility.
exp.1:8:
Paul says that women should dress in a decent way, with modesty and good sense. They should not depend on very elaborate hairstyles, nor on gold, pearls, or expensive clothing. The phrase "broided hair" in the verse refers to hair arranged in elaborate braids or curls, so the rewritten comment here is simply that elaborate hairstyles are not the point. The words "modest apparel" mean clothing that is dignified and appropriate, "shamefacedness" here means a sense of propriety, and "sobriety" means sound judgment and self-control.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his co-worker, who was leading the church in Ephesus. After speaking about the prayers of the men, he turns to the conduct of the women in worship. Some think he was correcting an excess of luxury or showiness in that community; the text gives no further details. The following verse clarifies that the true adornment is good works.

For today: before we get ready, we can ask ourselves whether we want to draw attention or to reflect a humble heart. May our greatest adornment be service and kindness.
exp.4:10:
Paul says that younger widows should not be placed on the list of widows the church supported. He says that when strong desires pull them away from their devotion to Christ, they want to marry. "Wanton" here means they become unrestrained or are carried away by their desires, and that draws them away from their commitment.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was overseeing the church in Ephesus. He was giving guidelines to help widows who had no means of support. The list included older women who devoted themselves to serving and praying. Scholars discuss what promise the younger women had made, but it seems to have been a commitment of service. Paul does not forbid marriage; in verse 14 he advises that younger women marry.

For today: before making a commitment before God, think calmly about whether you will be able to keep it. And when you support others, do so with wisdom, seeking what will truly help them.
exp.5:4:
It says there are people who argue without stopping. Their minds are damaged ("corrupt in mind") and they have lost the truth. They use faith as a business: "gain" means profit or financial advantage, and "godliness" means living with reverence for God. Paul ends with a clear command: "withdraw yourself from such," that is, stay away from them.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke of proud teachers who got caught up in word battles that caused envy and quarrels. Paul wants to protect the church. Then he clarifies that true gain is godliness accompanied by contentment.

For today: examine what you seek in your life of faith. If someone uses spiritual things to get rich or stir up fights, do not let yourself be dragged along. Seek God with a grateful heart and be content with what you have.
exp.2:11:
It says that deacons, that is, those who serve in the church, must be faithful to their wife, "husbands of one wife." They must also lead their children and their home well. "Ruling" here means guiding and caring with responsibility, not commanding harshly.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader in Ephesus, to teach him how to organize the church. Earlier he speaks of bishops or overseers, and then of deacons. He asks that they first be tested, so that service is entrusted to people of good reputation. Some understand "husband of one wife" as marital faithfulness; others debate whether it excludes the divorced. The phrase allows several interpretations.

For today: whoever serves in the church starts at home. Give time to your family, be faithful, and care for how you treat one another at home, because that is where the character is formed that later shows in service.
exp.5:6:
It says that we came into this world bringing nothing, and that we will not be able to take anything with us when we leave it. The phrase meaning "without a doubt" is one we can rely on, and the word for taking something away is the same idea as carrying it out. It is a reminder that possessions are temporary.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young coworker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he speaks of deceptive teachers who used religion as a business, using it to gain profit. Paul answers that true gain is living with faith and contentment, and then he warns against the love of money.

For today: before buying or wanting something more, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to God or only feeds your anxiety. Give thanks for what you already have, such as food and clothing, and share something with someone who needs it. In this way you practice the contentment that Paul teaches.
exp.1:4:
He says that there is one God and one mediator, that is, someone who joins two separated parties, between God and people. That mediator is Jesus Christ, who is also a man. "Likewise" means "also" or "in the same way": just as there is one God, there is one bridge to him.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, while giving him instructions for the church. Earlier he asked for prayers for everyone, because God wants all people to be saved and to know the truth. Then he explains that Jesus gave himself as a ransom for all. Paul mentions that he was appointed as a preacher and apostle to announce this message, especially to the Gentiles.

Today we can approach God with confidence, without feeling that we need other intermediaries or that we must earn merits of our own. You can pray today, just as you are, speaking to God in the name of Jesus, and encourage others to do so as well.
exp.2:9:
It says that those who aspire to be deacons must be examined first, before they begin to serve. If after that test there is nothing to accuse them of, then they may carry out their service. "Serve" means that they serve, and "without accusation" means without any serious charge against their conduct, that is, blameless.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was overseeing the church in Ephesus, and gives him guidelines for choosing leaders. Before this verse he mentions the character that deacons must have. The explanation does not detail how the test was carried out; some think it meant observing their conduct and their reputation in the community.

For today: before we give someone a responsibility in the church, let us give them time to show their character. And if we are the ones who want to serve, let our daily life speak first.
exp.4:2:
Paul asks Timothy to honour widows who are widows indeed. "Honour" here means to respect, value, and also help with what they need. "Widows indeed" refers to women who have been left alone, with no family to support them.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus, to give him guidance on how to treat different groups of believers. The verses that follow explain that if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should look after her first. The church was to care for those who were truly left without help and who put their trust in God.

For today: think of a widow or an older person who is alone in your church or your family. Call her, visit her, or help her with something concrete, such as a meal or an errand. In this way you show her that her life matters and that God has not forgotten her.
exp.4:21:
He tells Timothy not to lay hands on anyone in a hurry. "Lay hands suddenly" means doing it without thinking it through carefully. He also asks Timothy not to become a sharer in other people's sins and to keep himself pure.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who is caring for the church in Ephesus. Shortly before, he spoke about how to treat elders and those who sin. Laying on of hands probably refers to recognizing or setting someone apart for service in the church, though some also connect it with the restoration of a person who repented. Interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: before giving someone a responsibility in the church or in a group, take time, pray, and observe their character. And guard your own life so that you do not support what is wrong.
exp.4:17:
It says that those who work deserve to receive their pay. The phrase about not muzzling the ox that treads out the grain means that the ox should not have its mouth covered while it treads on the grain, since it also has a right to eat. The word for pay that is used here refers to the wage for one day's work.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke of honoring the elders who lead well, especially those who preach and teach. To support this idea he quotes Deuteronomy 25:4 and a saying similar to what Jesus said in Luke 10:7. Some understand "double honor" to include financial support; others think it refers mainly to respect. The verse favors the idea of provision.

Today we can support, with generosity and gratitude, those who serve in the church through teaching and caring for people, and treat them with respect.
exp.3:1:
This verse describes false teachers who speak lies while appearing pious. Speaking lies while pretending to be what one is not is the sense here. "Having their conscience seared" means that their conscience has been branded with a hot iron, like burned skin that no longer feels anything. These people no longer feel guilt when they deceive others.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He warns him that the Spirit had already announced that times of falling away would come. Some would turn away from the faith, and their teachings, such as forbidding marriage or certain foods, would sound very religious, yet they contradicted what God had made good.

Today we can examine what we hear in the light of the Bible, and take care of our own conscience. When the heart points out a wrong, it is wise to listen to it and correct ourselves quickly, so that we do not grow accustomed to what is wrong.
exp.5:13:
Paul asks Timothy to keep the commandment without spot and without blame, until our Lord Jesus Christ appears. "Without spot" means free from stain, and "unrebukeable" means that no one could rightly accuse him. "Appearing" refers to the coming of Christ.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was pastoring in Ephesus. He has just reminded him of his good confession of faith and of the example of Jesus before Pilate. It is not entirely clear which "commandment" he means: some think it is everything Paul entrusted to him in the letter, others that it is the call to live and serve faithfully. In either case, the sense is to persevere.

For today: live with integrity in what God has entrusted to you, whether your work, your family, or your service in the church. Ask for his help to be steadfast and honest, knowing that Christ will return.
exp.0:12:
Paul says that before he knew Christ he spoke against Him (a blasphemer), persecuted believers, and treated them with violence and contempt (injurious). But God had mercy on him, because he acted without knowing the truth, in unbelief. Paul's phrase about receiving mercy means that God showed him compassion instead of punishing him.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, out of his own experience as an apostle. He has just thanked Christ for putting him into the ministry. Now he recalls his past to show that his calling was a gift, not something he earned.

Some think that being ignorant does not excuse him, but rather explains why he received mercy; the text says nothing more.

Today, if your past weighs on you, remember that God's mercy is greater. And if you know someone who opposes the faith, do not lose hope: God can change anyone.
exp.4:5:
It says that a widow who gives herself over to pleasure and luxury, although she seems to be alive, is in reality dead. Death here is understood in a spiritual sense: a life without purpose or relationship with God.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Before this, he speaks about the widow who is truly alone, who trusts in God and prays night and day. By contrast, he warns about the widow who devotes herself only to herself. In this way he guides the church on whom to help and how to live responsibly.

Today we can ask ourselves what directs our lives: comfort, or love for God and for our neighbor? A simple step is to set aside a fixed time each day to pray and to serve someone.
exp.4:13:
Paul says that he wants the younger widows to marry again, have children, and take care of their homes. In this way they will give no reason to the adversary (anyone who opposes the faith) to speak reproachfully of believers. Here, "speak reproachfully" means to criticize or slander.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was overseeing the church in Ephesus. Earlier he had explained which widows the church should support. Younger women were not on that list, since they could fall into idleness and gossip, or abandon their commitment to Christ. It is practical advice for that situation, not a rule for all women.

For today: make sure that your way of living, your work, and your responsibilities at home give a good witness of your faith and offer no reason for others to speak against Christ.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that the foods God created are made holy, that is, set apart for a good use, "by the word of God and prayer." The word "meals" is used here, and the phrase about giving thanks means to thank God.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. There were false teachers who forbade marriage and certain foods. Paul answers that God's creation is good. The Bible affirms that God made things, and prayer acknowledges that they come from Him. Some understand "the word of God" as what God declared about creation; others, as the teaching of the Scriptures in general.

For today: before eating, or when enjoying any gift from God, pause and give thanks. In this way you receive with gratitude, without guilt or fear, what He gives you.
exp.1:6:
He states that he speaks the truth and does not lie. He teaches "in faith and verity," that is, with loyalty to God and with an authentic message.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was looking after the church in Ephesus. He has just spoken of Christ giving himself for everyone, and for that reason he stresses that his calling reaches people of every nation. His insistence that he does not lie probably strengthens his authority over those who were teaching different things, although the text gives no further details.

For today: if God has given you a task of teaching or advising others, do it with honesty and faithfulness. Speak the truth, without exaggerating or manipulating, and remember that the message of Christ is for everyone.
exp.5:18:
This verse says that the rich, by sharing and doing good, are laying up for themselves a good foundation for the future. In this way they can take hold of eternal life, that is, grasp it firmly. The word "storing up" here means gathering a treasure, and the older spelling of the preposition makes no difference to the meaning.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Before this verse, he asks Timothy to teach the rich not to be proud or to trust in money, but to trust in God. Paul does not say that generosity earns us salvation; other passages teach that it is a gift from God. Here he speaks of a life that shows true faith.

Today, we might ask ourselves: what do I trust more, what I have or God? This week, share something concrete, such as time, money, or help, with someone who needs it.
exp.1:14:
The explanation says that the woman will be saved through bearing children, provided she remains steady in faith, love (charity), a life set apart for God (holiness), and good judgment (modesty). All of these agree that what matters is a living faith.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was serving the church in Ephesus. He gives him instructions about conduct in the congregation and helps him correct mistaken teaching.

For today: whatever your stage or role in life, your worth and your salvation rest in God. Live with faith, love, and simplicity in everyday things, trusting that He sustains you.
exp.2:14:
This verse says that Paul is writing to Timothy in case he is delayed in arriving. He wants Timothy to know how he ought to conduct himself in the house of God. The word for conducting oneself, meaning to behave or live, is rendered in the King James Version as "behave thyself," and the phrase "as soon as" is rendered in the same way. The house of God is the church, the people of the living God, described as "the pillar and ground of the truth," that is, the one that upholds and displays the truth.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader in Ephesus. He gives instructions about the order and character of those who serve in the church. He hopes to visit him soon, but the letter will serve if he is delayed. Then he turns to speak of Christ, the center of the faith.

For today: take care how you speak and act in your church. Serve with humility, honesty, and respect, because as a community it upholds and displays God's truth to the world.
exp.4:4:
She says that the true widow is the one left alone, with no family to support her. That is why she places her hope in God and devotes herself to asking him for help with pleas and prayers, day and night. "Pleas" are requests made with persistence and humility. "Desolate" means she is alone, without support.

Paul writes to Timothy, his co-worker, who was overseeing the church in Ephesus. He gives guidance about whom the church should help. The verses before this one ask that children and grandchildren take care of their widows first. Here he describes the widow with no one, whose life of faith stands in contrast to the one who lives given over to pleasure (v. 6).

For today: we can walk alongside and support those who are alone, starting with our own family. And when we feel alone, we can make prayer a daily refuge, trusting that God hears us.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that no one should look down on Timothy because he is young, but that he should live in such a way that he becomes an example for the believers. He should be one in what he says ("word"), in how he lives (his "conversation," which in older English means conduct), in love ("charity"), in his spirit or attitude, in his faith, and in his purity ("cleanness").

Paul writes to Timothy, his youngest co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Paul does not know exactly when he will be able to return, so he encourages Timothy to teach with firmness. Scholars do not agree on Timothy's exact age, but he was young enough that some people looked down on him.

Today, do not wait until you are older to set a good example. And if you are older, value the young people who serve faithfully. Choose one of these areas today, such as your words or your purity, and ask God for help to live it consistently.
exp.4:9:
She is said to be well known for good works, which is why the church places such a widow on a special list. Her record includes raising children, showing hospitality (receiving and caring for others in her home), washing the feet of the saints (serving believers with humility), helping the afflicted (assisting those who suffer), and diligently following every good work.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was overseeing the church in Ephesus, and gives him guidelines for caring for widows. Here he describes what kind of widow should receive help and recognition. Scholars debate whether that list was only about financial help or also about service in the church; the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: faith shows itself in concrete service. Think of someone close to you who is suffering or in need of company, and help them this week with something simple and real.
exp.1:9:
It says that the true beauty of a Christian woman is not in her appearance but in her good works. The phrase continues what comes before it: not adorning herself with luxury, but with good works. "Becometh" means "is fitting." "Professing godliness" means they say they believe in God and give him reverence.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He wanted order and a good witness in the meetings. He asks that the men pray without anger and that the women not seek attention through luxuries. The verses that follow, about teaching and authority, are understood in several different ways among Christians.

For today: before you worry about how you look, think about whom you can help this week. A visit, a shared meal, or a concrete act of help shows your faith more than any ornament.
exp.0:8:
Paul says that the law is not made for someone who already lives in righteousness, but for those who live in rebellion: people who do not do what is right, who disobey, who despise God or what is holy, and even who kill their father, their mother, or others. The law restrains sin and makes it visible.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. There, some people wanted to be teachers of the law, but they used it wrongly and got lost in arguments. Paul makes clear that the law is good, but it must be used for its purpose. Some understand this as the law of Moses, others as the moral law in general.

Today, use the Bible first to examine yourself, not to judge others. Let it show you your need for Christ and lead you to his grace.
exp.4:3:
It says that if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to take good care of their own family out of reverence for God, and to give back to their parents or grandparents what they received from them. "Giving back" means returning in kind, repaying with care the good that was received. "Proper" here means right, worthy of approval. This pleases God.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who leads the church in Ephesus, about how to care for widows. Some had no one to support them. Paul teaches that the family should be the first to help, so that the church can truly support the widows who are left completely alone, as the verses that follow show.

Today, honoring God includes caring for our parents and grandparents as they grow old: visiting them, keeping them company, helping them financially where we can, and not leaving that responsibility to others.
exp.2:8:
It says that deacons must hold on to the truth of the Christian faith, which is called "mystery" because God made it known through revelation, and live it with a clear conscience. That is, what they believe and what they do should agree, without hidden guilt or duplicity.

Paul writes to Timothy, his co-worker, who was overseeing the church in Ephesus. He gives requirements for those who serve as deacons, people who helped with the practical service of the community. Before that, the text says they must not be "double-tongued," that is, people of double words, who say one thing to one person and another to someone else. Then it asks that they be tested before serving.

For today: it is not enough to know doctrine well; living with integrity matters too. If you serve in your church or anywhere else, try to be consistent, acknowledge your faults, and ask forgiveness from God and from others, so that you can serve with inner peace.
exp.2:4:
This verse asks a simple question: if someone does not know how to lead his own family well, how will he be able to take care of the church of God? "Rule" here means to direct, guide, and look after with responsibility. "Take care of" speaks of attending to something with diligence, like someone who watches over something precious.

Paul is writing to Timothy, whom he left in charge of the church in Ephesus. In this letter he lists the qualities of the one who aspires to be a bishop or overseer. The home works as a testing ground: there a person's real character shows, including his patience, his example, and the way he treats others.

For today: before seeking to serve or lead anywhere, take care of your home. Be steady, humble, and kind toward those who live with you. If you are single or live alone, practice that same character in your close relationships.
exp.0:15:
Paul says that God showed him mercy for a special reason: so that Jesus Christ might display in him, as the first case, all his patience and kindness. The word translated "mercy" in some versions means patience and compassion toward someone who does not deserve it. His story would be an example for everyone who would later believe in Christ and receive eternal life.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker in Ephesus. Before, he had been a persecutor of Christians, and here he remembers this with humility. He calls himself the foremost of sinners, perhaps because he was the clearest example of grace, or because of how he saw himself. He ends by praising God.

If God could transform Paul, no one is too far from his grace. Today you can draw near to God without hiding your past, and also treat with patience those who are still struggling, since God was patient with you.
exp.4:11:
This verse says that certain younger widows stand "having damnation," that is, under judgment or reproach, because they have "cast off" or broken their first faith. "Cast off" here means to break or void a commitment. The "first faith" most likely refers to the promise or commitment they had first made to Christ. Some think it was a vow to serve the church; others, simply their loyalty to Christ. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He gives guidance about which widows the church should support. The younger ones could be drawn by the desire to marry and give up the commitment to serve. Paul does not forbid marriage; in verse 14 he says he prefers that they marry.

For today: before promising something before God, think it over calmly and sincerely. And when you make a promise, keep it faithfully, asking the Lord for help.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that everything before it about the law and sound teaching agrees with the gospel of God's glory. Paul calls God "blessed," meaning worthy of praise and happy in himself. He says that this message was "committed to my trust," meaning entrusted to him as a responsibility.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He had been speaking about teachers who misused the law and about what goes against sound teaching. Here he says the right standard is the gospel, which he received as a treasure to guard and not to change. Right after this, he gives thanks because Christ, though Paul had once been a persecutor, treated him with mercy.

For today: if God entrusts us with his message, we should guard it with humility. We can read the Bible without twisting it and share it faithfully, remembering that everything comes from the grace of God.
exp.2:2:
This verse continues the list of qualities of a bishop, that is, a leader or overseer of the church. It says he must not be given to wine, nor a violent man, nor greedy for dishonest gain. He must be gentle and kind, not quarrelsome (someone who always argues or fights), nor a lover of money.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young coworker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He explains what character those who lead the community must have. What matters is not talent, but an upright life that serves as an example and protects the church.

Today, this invites us to examine our habits: how we handle money, our character, and our excesses. Whether or not we lead, God calls us to live with self-control, peace, and honesty in how we treat others.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that elders, that is, the leaders of the church, who lead well deserve special honor, meaning special respect and support. This applies especially to those who devote themselves with effort to preaching and teaching. The word "rule" means that they guide and care for the congregation.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, with instructions on how to organize the church. Earlier he spoke of helping widows in need; afterward he explains, using the example of the ox that treads out the grain, that whoever works deserves to be supported. Scholars debate whether "honor" includes financial payment, but the context suggests it does.

Today we can value those who teach us the Word: pray for them, thank them with concrete words, respect them and, as far as we are able, help them devote themselves to their work without anxiety.
exp.1:0:
Paul asks that, first of all, prayer be made for everyone. He uses four words: supplications (heartfelt pleading), prayers (speaking with God in general), petitions (asking for specific things) and thanksgivings (giving thanks). To exhort means to encourage or urge strongly. "All men" is understood to mean all people, without exception.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He gives him instructions on how to live and organize as a community. Placing prayer first among all things shows that it is a priority for the life of the church. The following verses mention those in authority and speak of God's desire for the salvation of all.

For today: make a short list of people you pray for rarely, such as neighbors, bosses, government leaders, or even people you don't like, and pray for them this week, asking for things and also giving thanks.
exp.3:0:
It says that the Holy Spirit speaks plainly: in future times, some people will fall away from the true faith. They will do so by paying attention to deceiving voices, and to teachings that come from demonic sources. The word "but" is the same as "yet", and "plainly" means "clearly".

Paul is writing to Timothy, a young leader of the church in Ephesus, to encourage him and to warn him. The verses that follow describe false teachers who forbid marriage and certain foods. Christians have understood the coming times in different ways: as the period between Christ and his return, or as a threat that was already beginning.

Today we can examine what we hear in the light of the Bible, without being carried away by what sounds spiritual or convincing. Knowing the Scriptures well and being in fellowship with other believers protects us from deception.
exp.4:23:
Some people's sins are clearly visible, even before they are judged. But the sins of others come to light later. Here "manifest" is rewritten as "clearly visible," and the phrase "at the time of being examined or judged" is simply translated, since the reader's verse says "going before to judgment."

Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader in the church, about how to choose and recognize leaders. He advises him not to rush in appointing someone to office (the laying on of hands), because true character is not always seen right away. The verses that follow say the same thing about good works: sooner or later they become known.

For today: do not judge people by a first impression. Take time to get to know them before giving them responsibilities, and live with integrity, trusting that God sees everything that is hidden.
exp.1:11:
Paul says that he does not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man, but that she should remain in quiet. The word "quiet" here is often understood as a calm and attentive attitude, not total muteness. "Authority" means to give orders or to dominate.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was in charge of the church in Ephesus. There were false teachers there and confusion (1 Timothy 1:3-7). The passage is about good order in worship. Christians interpret differently whether the instruction was meant for the local situation in Ephesus or is a rule for all churches. The verses that follow refer to Adam and Eve, and that is also understood in several ways.

For today: whatever your position on this subject, seek to serve in your church with humility and order, and study the passage in prayer, listening to brothers and sisters who think differently.
exp.1:10:
It says the woman should learn with a quiet and respectful attitude. "Quietness" here can mean stillness and calm, not necessarily saying nothing. The idea of "subjection" is a willingness to submit, to let oneself be taught and directed.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he speaks about prayer and about dressing with modesty. Then he restricts teaching with authority over a man, and he mentions Adam and Eve. Scholars disagree about whether this is a rule for all times or a response to particular problems in Ephesus. Still, notice that the woman is encouraged to learn, which was remarkable for that time.

For today: approach the teaching of the Word with humility, attentiveness and a desire to learn, whatever your place in the church. And if you have questions about this passage, study it calmly and together with your leaders.
exp.3:8:
He says that what Paul has just said is a trustworthy teaching and that everyone should be glad to accept it. "Faithful saying" means a message that can be trusted. "Worthy of all acceptation" means it deserves to be received gladly. "Of all" indicates that it is for any person at all.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader in the church at Ephesus, to encourage and guide him. He has just told him to turn away from useless myths and to train himself in godliness, that is, in living with reverence toward God. Some think the phrase points back to what was said in verse 8, and others think it points ahead to what follows in verse 10. Both readings are possible.

Today we can ask ourselves where we put the most effort. Caring for the body is good, but it is also worth training the heart: praying, reading the Bible, and obeying God every day.
exp.5:16:
This verse asks the rich "of this age," that is, of the present time, not to be haughty, meaning proud or looking down on others. It also tells them not to put their trust in the uncertainty of riches, because money can be lost. Their confidence should rest in the living God, who gives us generously all we need to enjoy with gratitude.

Paul writes to Timothy, his co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus, according to Christian tradition. Just before this verse, there is a praise of God as the eternal and sovereign King. Paul contrasts that power and permanence with the fragility of money. Then, in the verses that follow, he adds that the rich should do good and be generous.

For today: whether you have little or much, ask yourself what your peace rests on. Thank God for what you have, and this week look for a concrete way to share with someone who is in need.
exp.5:11:
Paul tells Timothy to fight the good fight of faith. It is not a war with weapons, but a steady perseverance in believing and living as a Christian. "Lay hold on" means to grip something firmly. "Whereunto" means "to which," so the phrase refers back to the eternal life. Eternal life is the life with God that he already received when he was called.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier, he had warned him about the love of money and asked him to flee from it and pursue righteousness, faith, and love. The "many witnesses" may refer to his baptism, his ordination, or another public confession; scholars interpret this in various ways.

Today, faith is lived day by day. Choose one concrete situation where you are tempted to give up or give in, and ask God for strength to remain faithful to Christ.
exp.1:2:
It says that praying for all people, including rulers, is good and pleases God. The word "supplications" refers to requests or pleas, and "giving of thanks" means expressing gratitude. God is called "our Saviour" because he is the one who saves.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He gives him instructions on how to live and worship. Before this verse, he asks for prayers for all people, and afterward he explains the reason: God desires that all people be saved and come to know the truth. Some scholars debate how to understand "all," but here it clearly includes people of every kind.

Today, we can choose someone who is hard to love, or an authority in your country, and pray for that person sincerely, asking for their good and that they come to know Jesus.
exp.0:17:
Paul says to Timothy, whom he loves like a son: "This charge I commit to you." The "prophecies that went before on you" are messages that were spoken about Timothy earlier, probably when he was set apart for service. The phrase about fighting a good fight means that he should fight well, like a soldier, for the cause of Christ. The word "according to" shows that this fight rests on what God had already said about him.

Paul writes to Timothy, who is in charge of the church in Ephesus. He has just praised God for his mercy. Now he gives him a firm command, because there were false teachers in Ephesus. We do not know in detail what those prophecies were; the text does not say.

For today: when you feel weak or doubt your calling, remember what God has done and said in your life. Lean on that, keep your faith and a good conscience, and keep serving with steadiness and humility.
exp.0:9:
This verse continues a list of people whom the law identifies as guilty. Here are named the fornicators (those who have sexual relations outside of marriage), the sodomites (an old term for sexual relations between men), the kidnappers (those who seized people to sell them as slaves), the liars, and those who swear falsely. It ends with an open phrase: anything else that is contrary to sound teaching, that is, to the instruction that gives spiritual life and health.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. There were teachers who used the law in a confused way and to no benefit. Paul explains that the law is good when it is used well: it shows sin and its seriousness, and so it points toward the gospel of grace.

For today: use the Bible to be guided, not to show off or to attack others. Let it examine your own heart first, and then announce with humility the good news that Christ forgives and transforms.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that whoever does not take care to provide for their relatives, and above all for those who live in their own household, has denied the faith by their actions. "His own" means their relatives; "infidel" here means someone who does not believe. In other words, even those who do not believe usually do not neglect their family in this way.

Paul is writing to Timothy, who was leading the church in Ephesus. Before and after this verse he speaks about how to care for widows. He asks that children and grandchildren look after their widows first, so that the church can help those who are truly alone.

For today: caring for one's family is part of living out the faith. Ask yourself whether there is a relative, such as an elderly parent or a sick family member, whom you could help with money, time, or companionship.
exp.1:5:
He says that Jesus Christ gave himself as the payment to set people free. "Ransom" was the price paid to win freedom for a slave or a prisoner. "For all" shows that his offering is for the whole of humanity. The idea of "to be testified in due time" means that this was a proof or sign from God, given at the moment he had chosen.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he asks for prayer for everyone, and here he explains the reason: God wants to save everyone, and Jesus is the only mediator between God and people. Then Paul says that he was appointed as a preacher and apostle to announce this message to the non-Jews.

For today: if Christ gave his life for all, we should not rule anyone out. Today you can pray for a person who is hard for you to love, asking that they come to know the truth and the love of God.
exp.3:6:
Paul tells Timothy to reject profane stories and fables, meaning tales that have no spiritual value, are worldly, and have no basis in the truth. Reject means to set aside or not accept. Instead of spending energy on such things, Timothy should train himself in godliness, that is, practice a life that honors God, the way someone trains every day.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who cares for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke to Timothy about false teachers with strange teachings. Now he reminds him that a good minister is nourished by faith and sound teaching. The expression about old wives was a way of saying these were unserious tales; it is not meant to insult elderly women.

Today we can choose what we listen to and read. Before giving time to rumors, odd theories, or pointless arguments, let us set aside a moment each day for the Bible and prayer, so that we grow in a life that pleases God.
exp.5:9:
It says that the love of money, that is, clinging to it with the heart, is the root of all kinds of evil. The word "coveted" in the verse means to desire eagerly. The phrase "have erred from the faith" means they wandered off the path of faith. "Pierced themselves through" speaks of being pierced, as with a sword, with many sorrows.

The apostle Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke of being content with the basics, and warned against those who want to get rich at any cost. Now he asks Timothy to flee that attitude and pursue righteousness, faith, and love. Paul does not say that money is evil, but the love of it.

Today, honestly ask yourself what place money holds in your heart. Practice contentment: give thanks for what you have, and give or help someone, so that money becomes your tool and not your master.
exp.1:1:
Paul asks that we pray for kings and for all those who hold authority. "Eminence" means a high position or a place of power, so that sentence should be rewritten: the phrase "a high position or a place of power" would be an explanation of an old word not in the verse, so delete it. "Honesty" here means a dignified and respectable way of living, so that sentence should be rewritten: the word "honesty" appears in the verse, and the explanation may stay as: "Honesty" here means a dignified and respectable way of living. The reason is so that we may live in peace and quiet, with reverence toward God and good conduct.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He gives him instructions about how to live and how to worship. The rulers of that time were not Christians and were sometimes hostile, but Paul still asks that we pray for them. The verses that follow connect this with God's desire that all people be saved.

For today: pray by name for your authorities, even if you do not agree with them. Ask God to guide them with wisdom and justice, and that you may be able to live in peace, respect, and a good testimony.
exp.5:10:
This verse tells Timothy to turn away from the love of money and the harmful desires that come with it, and to pursue with determination the qualities that please God: righteousness (living uprightly), godliness (reverence and love for God), faith (trust in Him), love (charity), patience (steady endurance), and meekness (a humble and gentle way of treating others). "Man of God" was a title given to God's servants and messengers.

The apostle Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader in the church at Ephesus. Earlier he spoke of the dangers of wanting to get rich at any cost. Now, with the words "But you," he marks the contrast: Timothy must live differently. He then encourages him to fight the good fight of faith.

For today: when you feel the pressure to live thinking only about having more, choose one of these virtues, such as patience or meekness, and practice it this week at work or at home. In this way your heart will become focused on what lasts.
exp.3:5:
He says that if Timothy teaches these things to the brothers, he will be a good servant of Jesus Christ. Timothy has been nourished on the words of the faith and on the good teaching that he has followed up to now.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier, Paul had spoken of false teachers who forbade certain foods and marriage. He answers that what God has made is good and is to be received with thanksgiving. Here he encourages Timothy to teach that truth with firmness and simplicity.

For today: whoever teaches or guides others, at home, in church, or with friends, needs first to be fed on the Word and prayer. Set aside a fixed time each day to read the Bible, so that what you share comes from a living faith and not from mere opinions.
exp.0:18:
Paul tells Timothy to keep holding on to faith and to keep a good conscience. Some people pushed their conscience away, and because of that they were shipwrecked in the faith, meaning their faith sank like a ship that is destroyed.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He reminds him to fight the good fight, that is, to serve with courage. As a warning example, he mentions Hymenaeus and Alexander, who turned away from the truth. Interpreters explain in different ways what it means to be handed over to Satan, but in general it is understood as a discipline meant to lead them to repentance.

For today: when you sense that something in your conscience is warning you, do not ignore it. Listen to it, confess it to God, and correct your course, so that your faith stays firm.
exp.2:5:
It says the one who oversees the church should not be a "novice," that is, someone who has only recently come to faith. The reason is that such a person might become puffed up, that is, filled with pride, and so fall into the same judgment that came upon the devil. That last phrase can be understood in two ways: the judgment God gave the devil for his pride, or the judgment the devil himself brings upon the proud. In both cases, the warning is against pride.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was helping the churches in Ephesus, and gives him requirements for bishops or overseers. Earlier he speaks of the leader's character and household. Now he warns that a position of authority is dangerous for someone who has not yet matured in the faith.

For today: let us not rush to take places of influence. Let character grow over time, and if we serve, let us do so with humility and willing to keep learning.
exp.3:15:
It says that Timothy must watch over his own life and over what he teaches, and not let go of either one. "Take heed" is "pay attention." "Continue" is "remain firm." "Á" is the old form of "a." "You will save" here speaks of being kept in the faith until the end, and of helping others to remain in it.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young leader who served in the church at Ephesus. Paul encourages him not to neglect the gift he received when the elders laid their hands on him. He asks him to be steadfast, because in that church there were false teachings and Timothy needed firmness.

For today: if you teach, serve, or guide others, do not care only for what you say. Care also for how you live. Set aside time each week to read the Bible, pray, and check whether your conduct matches what you teach.
exp.4:1:
It says that Timothy should treat older women with the respect one gives a mother, and younger women with the affection of a brother toward his sisters. The words "elder women" and "younger" refer to older and younger women in the church. "With all purity" means with complete cleanness of intention, without any doubtful or flirtatious conduct.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He wants to teach him to treat each group in the congregation as if they were family. That is why this verse follows what he said about older and younger men, and it prepares the topic of widows.

For today: in the church, treat each person as family. With those of the opposite sex, watch your words, your gestures, and your moments alone, so that everything is clean and honors God.
exp.5:5:
Here the explanation says that a life of faith in God (what the Bible calls "godliness") brings great gain when it goes together with contentment. The word that means "but" is translated here in the verse itself, and "gain" in the sense of profit or a worthwhile business refers to the gain mentioned in the verse. "Contentment" means being at peace and satisfied with what one has.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he had spoken about false teachers who used religion to make money and caused quarrels. Paul answers them that true gain is not having more, but knowing God and being satisfied. He then adds that we brought nothing into the world and we will take nothing out of it.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking God in order to get something, or whether He himself is our riches. This week, give thanks for the basics you already have, and resist the urge to compare yourself with others.
exp.3:2:
This verse says that some false teachers will forbid marriage and command people to abstain from certain foods. The phrase about giving thanks means giving thanks. Paul reminds us that God created those foods so that believers, who know the truth, may enjoy them with thanksgiving.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He warns him about false teachings that would come, and he calls them "teachings of demons" because they lead people away from the faith. It is not known exactly which group taught them, but the text shows that they added human rules. The verses that follow explain that what God has created is good.

For today: do not add rules that God never set, in an attempt to be more "spiritual." Receive with gratitude the good things God gives, such as family and food, and pray before you enjoy them.
exp.3:7:
It says that bodily exercise is worth "little," meaning it has limited value. By contrast, godliness, which is living with reverence and love for God, is worth "everything." It also brings a promise for the life we have now and for the life to come, that is, eternity. "Profits" here means it benefits.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young coworker who was caring for the church. He has just asked him to reject worldly myths and to train himself in godliness. Paul uses the image of training: just as the body is disciplined, the heart must be disciplined. He then says that it is because of this hope in the living God that they work and suffer.

For today: set aside a moment each day to pray and read the Bible, with the same consistency you would give to caring for your health. In this way your faith will grow little by little.
exp.2:0:
It says this is a trustworthy saying: if someone desires the office of bishop, they desire a good work. "Faithful saying" means something sure and true. "Desire" here means to want something eagerly. A "bishop" is someone who oversees and looks after the church; the Greek word speaks of an overseer. Here the verse speaks of a task, not a title of prestige.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, who served the church in Ephesus. He wants to guide him on how to set the life of the congregation in order. That is why, after encouraging this desire, he immediately lists the character that is expected: blameless, temperate, hospitable, able to teach. Scholars discuss exactly how "bishop" relates to "elder" or "pastor," though they are closely linked.

Today, desiring to serve others in the church is a good thing, but it is wise for that desire to go together with humility and a character that is cared for every day.
exp.0:7:
The explanation says that God's law is good, but with one condition: that it be used "lawfully," meaning in the right way and for the purpose for which it was given. "Yet" means "but." "Use it" means to apply it or make use of it.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was in Ephesus looking after the church. Some wanted to be teachers of the law, but they spoke without understanding and filled everyone with pointless arguments. Paul does not attack the law; he corrects those who were using it wrongly. Many understand its right use to be showing sin and pointing out our need for the gospel.

For today: use the Bible to be transformed and to love others better, not to win arguments or to judge others. Before you teach something, ask yourself whether you understand it well and whether you are doing so with humility.
exp.2:6:
He says that the overseer, or leader of the church, must also have a good reputation among those who do not believe. The words "those outside" refer to people who are not part of the church. "Disgrace" means shame or loss of respect, and a "snare" is a trap, like the ones set to catch animals. So the leader avoids falling into dishonor and into a trap of the devil.

Paul writes to Timothy, his co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He gives the qualities that a leader should have. Earlier he spoke of managing one's own household well and of not being a new convert. Some understand "the snare of the devil" as the trap the devil sets for the leader; others, as the trap the devil uses through a bad reputation. The text allows both readings.

For today: take care of your witness where you work and live. Pay your debts, keep your word, and treat everyone with respect, because your conduct speaks of the Lord.
exp.2:7:
Paul says that deacons must be serious people who deserve respect. The word "doubletongued" here does not refer to languages, but to saying one thing to one person and something different to another. They must also avoid excess wine and not pursue money through dishonest means.

Paul writes to Timothy, his co-worker, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He gives him instructions for good order in the community. After speaking about the overseers or elders, he describes the deacons, whose name means "servants." Since they attended to the needs of the church, their character had to inspire trust. Scholars do not fully agree on what their exact duties were.

Today, whatever your service in the church, watch your words and how you handle money. Be the same person in front of everyone, keep what you promise, and be honest with what is entrusted to you.
exp.0:2:
Paul reminds Timothy that he had asked him to stay in Ephesus while Paul travelled on to Macedonia. The task was to command certain people with authority and warn them not to teach any doctrine different from the one they had received.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, whom he calls his true son in the faith. The church in Ephesus was facing teachers who were drifting away from the gospel. The verses that follow speak of myths and endless genealogies that caused arguments. Paul wants Timothy to take care of sound teaching.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with what the Bible says. And if you have a responsibility to guide others, do it with firmness and love, always seeking to build up faith and not just to argue.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the goal of everything God commands is love. The word "end" here means purpose or goal, and "charity" means love. That love comes from three things: a pure heart, a good conscience, and a faith that is genuine. Saying "unfeigned" means that the faith is not false or merely for show.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young coworker, who was in Ephesus. Some people there were teaching things different from the gospel and getting lost in arguments about myths and endless lists of ancestors. Paul reminds Timothy that true teaching aims to form people who love, not to win debates.

For today: before arguing about faith, ask yourself whether what you say and do comes from a sincere heart and produces love toward others. Ask God to cleanse your heart and give you a real faith, not one that is only for show.
exp.0:3:
Paul tells Timothy not to let people busy themselves with "fables" (invented stories) or with endless lists of ancestors. The word "á" is simply "to," and "questions" means arguments and quarrels. These things produce debate, but they do not help build up the spiritual life that God works through faith. "So do" means: "this is what I am commanding you."

Paul writes to Timothy, his son in the faith, who stayed behind in Ephesus. Some there were teaching different doctrines. We do not know exactly what those fables and genealogies were; some think of Jewish traditions, others of ideas mixed with speculation. Paul wants the teaching to lead to love, to a pure heart, and to a sincere faith.

Today we can ask ourselves: does this conversation or teaching draw me closer to God and help me love better, or does it only feed arguments and curiosity? Let us choose what builds up.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that the mystery of our faith, which was hidden before and which God has now revealed to us, is great and beyond dispute. It speaks of Jesus: God became human ("God was manifest in the flesh"), he was vindicated as righteous by the Spirit, angels saw him, he was proclaimed to the non-Jewish nations ("the Gentiles"), many believed in him in the world, and he was taken up into glory. "Godliness" here means a life of faith and reverence toward God.
