Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was leading the church in Ephesus. He has just explained how to conduct oneself in the church, "the pillar and ground of the truth." This verse seems to be a brief confession or hymn that summarizes what that truth rests on. Some scholars believe it was a song of the early Christians, although this cannot be known for certain.

For today: when you doubt or feel weary, return to Jesus. Read the Gospels and let his life remind you that God truly drew near to you.
exp.2:13:
Paul tells Timothy that he is writing this letter in the hope of coming to see him soon. The word "shortly" means "soon" or "quickly." Note also that the verse reads "unto," which is an older way of saying "to."

Paul is the one speaking, and Timothy is the young leader who is caring for the church in Ephesus. Paul has already given him instructions about the leaders and the order of the church. Since he is not sure how long it will take him to arrive, he puts everything in writing so that Timothy knows how to conduct himself in the house of God.

For today: even when we cannot always be present, we can encourage and guide others with written words, a message, or a letter. A sincere and clear word can strengthen the faith of someone who needs direction.
exp.5:7:
It says that if we have food and clothing, we should be content with them. "Food" means nourishment and what is necessary to live. The phrase "clothing" refers to garments, and some understand that it also includes shelter. Being "content" means satisfied, without complaining or anxiety.

The apostle Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Earlier he speaks of godliness with contentment as true gain, and then he warns about the danger of wanting to become rich. Paul does not condemn having possessions, but warns against letting the desire for more take control of us and pull us away from the faith.

For today: before buying something you do not need, stop and thank God for what you already have. Practicing gratitude every day helps you cultivate a content heart that is less enslaved to money.
exp.4:14:
Some of these young widows, he says, had already turned away from the path of Christ and were following Satan. In other words, they had turned their backs on their faith and on the way they were living. The phrase "turned aside after" means giving up one road in order to follow another.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus, about how to look after the widows. According to him, the young widows could fall into idleness and gossip, and in this way harm the church's witness. For this reason he encourages them to marry and to take care of their homes. Scholars do not agree on the exact details of what was happening, but the advice aims to protect the faith and the reputation of the church.

For today: let us take care how we use our time and our words. Keeping busy with something good and speaking with respect helps us avoid opening the door to evil.
exp.5:0:
The explanation says that servants or slaves, those who live "under the yoke" (like a heavy load), should treat their masters with respect and honor. "Á" is the old form of "a," and "be blasphemed" means that it should not be spoken of with contempt. The reason is that their conduct should not bring dishonor to the name of God or to the Christian teaching.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus, with instructions for the life of the congregation. At that time slavery was common in the Roman world. Paul neither approves nor condemns the system here; his concern is that believers give a good witness in their actual situation. Christians are not the only ones in view in this context: the Bible teaches limits for masters in other passages.

Today, in our work, we can act with respect, honesty and good effort, even with difficult bosses, so that our conduct honors Christ.
exp.0:19:
It says that Hymenaeus and Alexander are two of those who abandoned a good conscience and suffered shipwreck in the faith. Paul says that he "handed them over to Satan." The word "handed" is simply how the verse reads here. The purpose was not to destroy them, but that they "may learn not to blaspheme," that is, to stop speaking evil of God and of the truth.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker in Ephesus, to encourage him to take care of sound teaching. These men had strayed. Handing them over to Satan probably refers to removing them from the Christian community, so that they would live without its protection and come to their senses. Some interpret it in other ways, and the text gives no further details.

For today: take care of your conscience and your faith. If someone turns away, correct them with humility and with the hope that they will return.
exp.5:14:
This verse says that the appearing of Jesus Christ, mentioned just before, will take place "in his own time," that is, at the moment God has decided. The one who will bring it about is God himself, who is described as "the blessed and only Potentate" (happy and complete), the one with absolute power alone, and "King of kings and Lord of lords" (above every ruler). The word "shew" means that he will make it visible.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He asks him to remain faithful and blameless until Christ appears. Then he praises God, and immediately gives instructions to the rich. Many understand that "which" refers to the appearing of Christ.

For today: if God holds time and power in his hands, we can obey him with patience and trust, without being anxious about what we do not control or leaning on what is uncertain.
exp.0:6:
It says that some wanted to be "doctores de la ley," that is, teachers of the teachings of Moses, but they did not understand what they were saying or what they insisted on so firmly. They spoke with confidence, but without real knowledge.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was in Ephesus, to correct certain teachers who had turned away from love, a good conscience, and sincere faith. They got lost in pointless arguments and wanted to appear wise. Paul makes clear right away that the law is good, but it must be used well.

Today it invites us not to teach or give opinions about the Bible with more confidence than knowledge. Before explaining something to others, it is wise to study it with humility and ask ourselves whether our teaching produces love and a clean conscience.
exp.0:13:
What it says: Paul affirms that the grace of God, that is, his undeserved favor, was exceedingly abundant in his life. That grace came together with the faith and love that are found in Christ Jesus. The word "was" in the older wording is simply the past tense of the verb, and "exceeding abundant" means that it went beyond every measure.

Context: Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker. He has just recalled that he once blasphemed against Christ and persecuted believers. Even so, God forgave him and placed him in ministry. Paul is not boasting about himself; he wants to show that God's grace was greater than his sin.

For today: If you carry guilt over your past, remember that the grace of Christ is greater than your mistakes. Come before God with sincerity, receive his forgiveness, and let his faith and love transform you and move you to serve others.
exp.3:13:
It says that Timothy must not neglect the gift God gave him. That gift was confirmed through a prophetic word and when the elders of the church laid their hands on him. "Neglect" means not paying attention to something, letting go of something valuable.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young coworker, who cares for the church in Ephesus. Paul wants to encourage him to carry out his service with firmness, even though he is young. We do not know in detail what that prophecy was or exactly what the gift was, but the text shows that the church recognized it and supported him.

For today: think about an ability or service that God has given you, such as teaching, helping, or encouraging. Set aside time for it each week, pray about it, and use it for the good of others, without letting fear or routine put it out.
exp.0:0:
Paul presents himself as an apostle, that is, one sent by Jesus Christ. He says he is one "by the commandment of God," meaning by the command or appointment of God, whom he calls our Saviour. He also calls Jesus Christ "our hope": it is in him that we trust for the future.

Paul writes this letter to Timothy, his young co-worker, whom he loved as a son in the faith. He begins by affirming his authority, because Timothy was in Ephesus correcting false teachings. A church with problems needed a message that came from God, not just from a man. As the letter itself says, that is the reason for the assignment.

For today: our calling and our confidence do not rest on our own strength, but on God's call and on Christ, our hope. When you feel unsure about what you are doing to serve, remember who called you and in whom you trust.
exp.5:2:
This verse speaks of someone who teaches something different and does not agree with the wholesome words of Jesus Christ, that is, with his true and healthy teachings. Nor does such a person accept the teaching that leads to living in reverence for God. "Agree" means "to agree," and "godliness" is a life that honors God.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just given instructions about how to live out the faith in everyday life, including the relationship between servants and masters. Now he warns that there are teachers who turn away from that simple teaching, and in the verses that follow he describes the harm they cause.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with what Jesus said and see whether it produces a life of love and reverence for God. If it only produces pride, quarrels, or profit, be wary.
exp.5:1:
Paul speaks to slaves whose masters are also believers. He tells them not to treat their masters with less respect just because they are now brothers in the faith. On the contrary, they should serve them even better, because those who receive their work are beloved brothers and share in the same benefit, which here is understood as God's grace and goodness. The phrase meaning "with less respect" refers to treating someone with contempt. The phrase about sharing in the benefit can refer to the service received or to God's favor; scholars interpret it in both ways.

Paul writes to Timothy, a young pastor in Ephesus, giving him instructions for the church. In that world slavery was common, and the Christian faith placed slaves and masters on equal footing before God. Paul does not defend the system; rather, he cares for the church's witness, so that no one speaks evil of the name of God.

Today, being brothers in the faith is no excuse for demanding less respect or effort. If you work alongside other believers, serve them with more dedication, not less, because your work honors Christ.
exp.5:15:
This verse says that God alone has immortality, meaning that he does not die and cannot die. He lives in a light so intense that no one can come near him. No person has seen him or can see him in his fullness. The word "everlasting" in the verse means that his honor and power last forever, and "dominion" refers to his power and authority.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. Just before this verse he speaks of the coming of Christ, and Paul bursts into praise as he describes the greatness of the God who will bring it about. Afterward, he returns to practical instructions about riches. Some think it is a hymn or a phrase of worship used in the church, though this is not certain.

For today: when you feel small or weighed down by your worries, remember who God is. Take a moment to worship him, and trust that he, so great and eternal, takes care of you.
exp.4:18:
It says that Timothy should not accept an accusation against an elder of the church unless two or three witnesses confirm it. "Elder" refers to a leader or pastor of the congregation. The sentence "do not receive" means not admitting it or treating it as valid. It is a safeguard against rumors and attacks without proof.

Paul writes to Timothy, his young co-worker, who is caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just spoken of honoring and supporting the elders who work well. Now he adds that they also deserve justice. This rule recalls the law of Moses about witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). Afterward, Paul asks that whoever keeps on sinning be rebuked publicly, without favoritism.

For today: let us not repeat or create criticism against a leader without checking it. If someone makes an accusation, let us seek facts and witnesses, with justice and without partiality.
exp.1:3:
It says that God desires that all people be saved and come to know the truth, that is, the message of the gospel about Jesus Christ. "Men" here means human beings in general. "Will" expresses his desire and his heart. Christians have understood in different ways how this desire of God relates to his sovereignty and to human freedom, but all agree that it shows his love.

Paul writes to Timothy, who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just asked for prayer for all people, even for kings and authorities. The reason is that God, our Savior, desires the salvation of everyone, and then he reminds us that Jesus, the only mediator, gave himself for all.

For today: pray for people who are hard for you to love, such as bosses, authorities, or difficult neighbors. If God desires their salvation, you too can ask for it and share the truth with them kindly.
exp.4:12:
It says that some younger widows, when they have no work to occupy them, get into the habit of idleness and of going from house to house. Moreover, they become "gossips," who talk too much, and "busybodies," who meddle in other people's affairs, saying things that are not fitting.

Paul writes to Timothy, his co-worker who was overseeing the church in Ephesus, with instructions on how to care for widows. The church helped older widows who were left alone, but Paul advises not to include the younger ones on that list. His concern is that they have an orderly life and a good testimony. Some details of the previous verse are understood in different ways.

For today: unused free time without purpose can lead us into gossip. Let us look for a useful occupation, such as serving, working, or caring for others, and take care that our words build others up.
exp.5:20:
It says that some people, while proclaiming what Paul calls "falsely named knowledge," turned away from the faith, that is, they strayed from the right path. The word "professing" means declaring that one has or practices something. "Going astray" means being lost, off the path. Paul closes with a blessing: "Grace be with you." The final note about Laodicea is not part of the original text; it was added later by copyists, and its accuracy is disputed.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just asked him to guard the teaching he received and to avoid empty arguments and false knowledge. This is his final warning: some had already turned away from the faith by following those ideas.

For today: not everything that sounds intelligent or spiritual is true. Before accepting a teaching, compare it with what Jesus and the Bible say. And remember that to stay firm, you need God's grace more than your own strength.
exp.0:11:
Paul thanks Christ Jesus, "who hath enabled me," that is, the one who gave him strength and ability. He says that Christ "counted me faithful," meaning he considered him trustworthy, and for that reason put him into the ministry, which is a service to God and to people.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who was caring for the church in Ephesus. He has just spoken of the gospel that God entrusted to him. Now he pauses to give thanks, and in the verses that follow he recalls that he was once a blasphemer and a persecutor, but he received mercy.

For today: if God has given you some task, whether great or small, remember that you do not carry it out by your own strength alone. Give thanks to Christ, who strengthens you, and serve with humility.
exp.5:12:
Paul gives Timothy a solemn charge, as someone speaking before witnesses. He does so in the sight of God, who gives life to all things, and before Jesus Christ. He "witnessed a good confession" before Pontius Pilate, that is, he openly declared the truth about who he was with courage.

Paul, now an older man, writes to Timothy, the young leader of the church in Ephesus. He has just asked him to flee the love of money and to pursue righteousness and faith. Now he reminds him that his calling is lived under the gaze of God. He sets Jesus before him as the example of faithfulness, even in the face of a trial that would lead him to the cross.

For today: when it is hard to be faithful at work, at home, or at school, remember that God sees you and that Jesus has already walked that road. Ask him for the courage to speak the truth with love and to stand firm.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that those who keep living in sin must be corrected firmly and in front of everyone. The purpose is that others may have fear, that is, a serious respect for God and for sin.

Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker who leads the church in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke about how to treat the elders and about not accepting accusations without witnesses. For that reason, this verse is understood within a fair process. Many think it refers to proven sins of leaders, although some apply it to any believer.

For today: if a serious, proven sin must be corrected, it should be done with truth, justice, and love, seeking to heal and protect the community, never to humiliate anyone or spread gossip.
exp.0:14:
It says this message is trustworthy and deserves to be accepted by everyone: Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners. Paul adds that he considers himself the first among them. A trustworthy statement means a declaration that can be relied on, and the word "to" in the old spelling "á" is simply the ordinary word "to" in modern English.

The apostle Paul is writing to Timothy, his young co-worker. Before he came to know Christ, Paul had blasphemed and persecuted believers. He remembers his past not to punish himself, but to show that God's mercy was greater than his guilt. His story is proof that God can save anyone.

Today, you do not have to hide your mistakes or believe it is too late for you. Come to Jesus with humility and sincerity, and receive his forgiveness. Then, tell others with joy what he has done in your life.

sum.1: Paul asks that prayers be offered for everyone, including those in authority, because God wants all people to be saved and Jesus Christ is the only mediator, the one who gave himself as a ransom. He then gives instructions for worship: men are to pray without anger, and women are to live with modesty and good works. He also places limits on women's role in teaching, a passage that is interpreted in several different ways.
sum.0: Paul is writing to Timothy, who is in Ephesus, and asks him to correct those who teach false doctrines and get caught up in endless arguments. Paul gives thanks because God showed mercy to him, even though he was a great sinner, since Christ came into the world to save sinners. He encourages Timothy to hold on to faith and a good conscience.
sum.3: Paul warns Timothy that in the latter times some will abandon the faith and follow false teachings, such as forbidding marriage or certain foods, although everything God created is good when received with thanksgiving. He asks Timothy to train himself in godliness, to be an example despite his youth, and to take care of his own life and his teaching.
sum.4: Paul teaches Timothy to treat every person in the church with respect, as if they were family, and to care for widows who are truly in need, since the family should look after its own first. He also asks that elders who lead well be honored, that accusations be handled fairly, and that Timothy keep himself pure.
sum.5: Paul teaches Timothy to honor those in authority and to reject those who teach false things out of ambition. He warns that the love of money brings many evils, and that godliness with contentment is great gain. He encourages Timothy to fight the good fight of the faith, and he asks the rich to be generous and to trust in God.
sum.2: Paul explains to Timothy what overseers and deacons should be like: people of integrity, self-controlled, faithful in their homes and with a good reputation, who serve with a clear conscience. He says that the church is the pillar and foundation of the truth, and he closes with a hymn about the great mystery of Christ, revealed in the flesh and received in glory.
